examples.knowledge_point: Integrating a Trigonometric Expression Using Identities and Substitution
examples.worked_solution:
We use the identity $\tan 2x = \dfrac{\sin 2x}{\cos 2x}$ and rewrite the integral as

$$
\int \tan{2x}\,\textrm d x = \int \dfrac{\sin{2x}}{\cos 2x}\,\textrm d x.
$$

Notice that the numerator of the integrand is proportional to the derivative of the denominator. So, we can solve this by substitution.

Let $u=\cos 2x.$ Then

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm{d}x}=-2 \sin 2x \quad\Longrightarrow\quad -\dfrac 1 2 \,\textrm d u= \sin 2x \, \textrm d x.
$$

Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡2x}{\operatorname{cos}⁡2x}\,\text{d}x & =-\frac{1}{2}\int \frac{1}{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡|u|+C \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡|\operatorname{cos}⁡2x|+C \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡|(\operatorname{cos}⁡2x)^{-1}|+C \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡|\operatorname{sec}⁡2x|+C\end{aligned}
$$

feedback.worked_solution:
We can write the integral as

$$
{\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{{cos}^{2}⁡x}\text{d}x={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}\frac{1}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}\cdot \frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}\,\text{d}x
$$

We use the fact that $\frac{1}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}=\operatorname{sec}⁡x$ and $\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}=\operatorname{tan}⁡x$ to express this as

$$
{\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}\operatorname{sec}⁡x\operatorname{tan}⁡x\,\text{d}x.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{{cos}^{2}⁡x}\text{d}x & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}\operatorname{sec}⁡x\operatorname{tan}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & =\operatorname{sec}⁡x{|}_{0}^{\pi /4} \\  & =(\operatorname{sec}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4})-\operatorname{sec}⁡(0)) \\  & =\sqrt{2}-1.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$
